subject: Anatomy
summary: The pectoralis major is a large, fan‑shaped chest muscle that adducts and medially rotates the humerus. Its anatomy guides safe chest‑tube placement and explains injuries like tears or Poland syndrome.

sections.p: The pectoralis major forms the bulk of the anterior chest wall and is essential for upper‑limb movement and for protecting thoracic structures.
b: Origin: clavicular head (medial half of clavicle), sternocostal head (sternum, ribs 1‑6, and aponeurosis of external oblique).
Insertion: lateral lip of the bicipital groove of the humerus.

sections.p: It lies superficial to the pectoralis minor and deep to subcutaneous tissue, creating the anterior axillary line.
b: Divided into clavicular and sternocostal portions with distinct fiber directions.
Forms the anterior border of the safe triangle for chest‑tube insertion.

sections.p: Medially it contacts the sternum and ribs; laterally it blends with the deltoid; posteriorly the pectoralis minor lies deep.
b: Latissimus dorsi forms the posterior border of the safe triangle.
Axillary vessels and brachial plexus run deep to the muscle.

sections.p: Supplied mainly by the thoracoacromial artery (pectoral branch) and the lateral thoracic artery.
b: Collateral flow from internal mammary perforators.

t.b: Is arterial flow present? → Confirms patency; absent flow suggests injury or thrombosis.

sections.p: Innervated by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C5‑T1).
b: Medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor to reach the sternocostal head.
Lateral pectoral nerve supplies the clavicular head.

t.b: Is muscle activation normal? → Detects nerve injury; absent potentials indicate denervation.

sections.p: Produces powerful adduction and medial rotation of the humerus; assists in deep inspiration by raising the rib cage.
b: Clavicular head: flexes the arm at the shoulder.
Sternocostal head: draws the arm backward (horizontal adduction).

sections.p: Understanding its anatomy prevents complications during procedures and guides management of tears, atrophy, or congenital absence.
b: Chest‑tube insertion: stay within the safe triangle (pectoralis major‑latissimus dorsi‑5th intercostal space).
Pectoralis major rupture: sudden tearing pain during bench press; loss of adduction strength.
Poland syndrome: congenital absence, may need reconstructive surgery.

t.b: Is there a tendon tear? → Shows muscle retraction and edema; guides surgical vs. conservative care.
Is adduction/medial rotation weakened? → Indicates partial or complete rupture.

sections.p: Key points to remember for OSCEs and written exams.
b: Safe triangle boundaries: pectoralis major (anterior), latissimus dorsi (posterior), 5th intercostal space (inferior).
Two actions: adduction and medial rotation of the humerus.
Poland syndrome often coexists with hand anomalies (symbrachydactyly).

whenToSeekHelp: Severe chest‑tube malposition causing pneumothorax or hemorrhage
Complete pectoralis major rupture with neurovascular compromise
Rapidly expanding breast mass in Poland syndrome suggesting malignancy

faq.q: Why is the pectoralis major important for chest‑tube placement?
faq.a: It forms the anterior border of the safe triangle; staying behind it avoids cutting the thick muscle and protects neurovascular structures.

faq.q: What distinguishes a pectoralis major tear from a shoulder dislocation?
faq.a: A tear causes localized anterior chest pain and loss of adduction strength, while dislocation presents with shoulder deformity and limited range of motion.

faq.q: Can pectoralis major atrophy be caused by infection?
faq.a: Yes, chronic HIV or TB can lead to muscle wasting, and opportunistic infections may involve the muscle directly.

exam: Describe the boundaries of the safe triangle for chest‑tube insertion and why the pectoralis major is a landmark.
Explain the clinical presentation and imaging findings of a pectoralis major rupture.
List the nerve supply to the pectoralis major and the implications of an injury to each branch.
